trials.notes: Correctly used WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for flat source-order work, walked matching H2 tags with documented next_tag('h2'), moved one bookmark to each match, sought back, used add_class(), and returned get_updated_html(). All called APIs are documented and execution recorded no _doing_it_wrong entries.

Same correct documented pattern as the reference, with has_bookmark() and release_bookmark(). Processor choice, bookmark usage, class mutation, and output retrieval all match the rendered docs. No undocumented calls or _doing_it_wrong records.

Correct flat-scan implementation using documented APIs only. Re-setting the same bookmark on every H2 match exactly follows the docs' last-match idiom; add_class() preserves existing classes. No API misuse was reported.

failure_analysis: All trials passed all 6 hidden cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to a misconception. The docs worked well here: the Tag Processor overview explicitly says to use WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for flat source-order tasks like first/last/Nth matching tags; next_tag() documents string tag-name queries, ASCII case-insensitive matching, comments/raw text not matching as tags, and incomplete-token behavior; set_bookmark() explicitly describes re-setting the same bookmark name to remember the last matching tag; add_class() documents appending to existing class attributes; and get_updated_html() is clearly described as the way to retrieve queued mutations. Near-misses were minor: trial-1 used a separate boolean instead of has_bookmark() and did not release the bookmark, but both are harmless for this short-lived processor and consistent with the reference behavior. None of the candidates confused serialization with mutation output or chose the tree-aware processor unnecessarily.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say to release bookmarks when no longer needed, but do not distinguish long-lived scans from short-lived processors where object destruction immediately follows.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify bookmark lifetime: releasing is useful before continuing a long scan or applying many later updates; at normal function exit it is optional because the processor is discarded.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs describe that next_tag() returning false can mean either not found or paused at incomplete input, but the last-match bookmark idiom does not remind readers to decide whether truncation matters to their contract.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general note to full-scan recipes: after scanning to false, check paused_at_incomplete_token() when the caller must distinguish a complete scan from truncated trailing syntax; otherwise only complete matched tokens are considered.

doc_gaps.problem: The method is documented only as an existence check, while the common conditional-scan use case is left implicit.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a small generic example showing has_bookmark() after a loop that conditionally sets a fixed bookmark name, as an alternative to maintaining a separate found flag.
